Your reputation is what other people collectively think and say about you — the general opinion that exists about you in other people's minds, based on your past actions, behavior, and track record over time.

It is not what you think about yourself. It is not what one person thinks about you. It is the shared, common belief that a group of people hold about you — and that belief gets passed from person to person through talk, observation, and experience.

Imagine you live in a neighborhood. Over the years, you always keep your promises, you help others, and you are honest in your dealings. People talk. Word spreads. Eventually, nearly everyone in that neighborhood thinks of you as a reliable, trustworthy person. That shared opinion — that general image of you in the community's mind — is your reputation.

Now imagine the opposite: someone who regularly cheats, lies, and lets people down. The same process happens in reverse. People talk, and the community forms a shared negative opinion. That too is a reputation.

The key idea: reputation lives in other people's minds, not your own.

A reputation is built from:

  • Repeated actions — not one event, but a pattern. One kind act doesn't make you kind. A history of kind acts does.
  • What others observe — people form opinions based on what they see, hear, or experience from you.
  • What others say — once people form opinions, they share them. This is how a reputation spreads beyond those who know you directly.

This is important: a reputation is shaped by reality (what you actually do), but also by perception (what people believe you do). Sometimes these match perfectly. Sometimes they don't — a person can have a good reputation they don't deserve, or a bad one that is unfair.

A reputation is not always purely good or purely bad. It can be:

  • A good reputation — people generally think well of you: "She has a reputation for being fair and honest."
  • A bad reputation — people generally think poorly of you: "He has a reputation for being unreliable."
  • A mixed reputation — people hold conflicting views: "The restaurant has a reputation for amazing food but terrible service."
  • A strong/solid reputation — the opinion is well-established and hard to shake.
  • A damaged reputation — something happened that harmed the previously good opinion people held.
Who or What Can Have a Reputation

Reputation doesn't only apply to people. Any entity that acts in the world and is observed by others can have one:

  • A person — a politician, a teacher, a doctor, a neighbor.
  • A company or organization — "Apple has a reputation for sleek, well-designed products."
  • A place — "That city has a reputation for being expensive."
  • A product — "This brand has a reputation for lasting a long time."
  • A profession — "Lawyers sometimes have a reputation for being difficult to understand."
How It Is Used in Sentences

• "She worked hard to build her reputation as a skilled surgeon."
  • "His reputation suffered after the scandal."
  • "The school has a reputation for academic excellence."
  • "Don't risk your reputation for a small gain."
  • "He has a reputation for always being late."
  • "It took her years to repair her damaged reputation."

You will often see it paired with these words: build, earn, protect, damage, ruin, destroy, repair, lose, maintain, establish, have, gain.
A Critical Feature: It Takes Time, But Can Be Lost Quickly

One of the most important things to understand about reputation is its fragility and slowness.

  • It takes a long time to build. A strong reputation is the result of consistent behavior over months or years.
  • It can be destroyed very quickly. One serious mistake, scandal, or betrayal can erase years of goodwill.

This is why people say things like "Your reputation is your most valuable asset" or "It takes a lifetime to build a reputation and a moment to ruin it."
How Reputation Differs from Similar Words

Since you are a learner, it helps to know how reputation differs from words that feel similar:

  • Character is who you actually are on the inside — your values, morals, and principles. Reputation is what people think you are. A person of good character might have a bad reputation (if people misunderstand them), and someone with a good reputation might have poor character (if they are secretly dishonest). Character is internal; reputation is external.
  • Fame means many people know of you or have heard of you. It is about being widely known. Reputation is about what people think of you once they know of you. A famous person can have a bad reputation. The two are separate things.
  • Image is very similar to reputation, but image often implies something more deliberately constructed or managed — the picture someone tries to project. Reputation feels more like a natural accumulation of what others genuinely think. A politician might carefully manage their image, but their reputation is what the public actually believes about them underneath the management.
  • Prestige is a form of high reputation, specifically involving admiration, status, and respect in a particular field or social circle. It is a kind of reputation — a specifically high-status one.

At its deepest level, reputation is about social trust. Human society runs on trust — we need to know who to rely on, who to hire, who to do business with, who to befriend. Reputation is the system by which that information is stored and shared in a community. It is your social track record.

When someone says "Your reputation precedes you," they mean that people already know what to expect from you before you even arrive — your reputation has traveled ahead of you and introduced you before you could introduce yourself.

This is why reputation matters so much in professional life, social life, and business: it determines whether people will trust you, work with you, buy from you, or recommend you — often before they even meet you.
